Pepsi Share of North America Distribution
Management reframed a recent slowdown in scanner-data growth as a comp and channel-timing issue, not a structural demand problem.
Emphasized 11.5% energy-category share (up four points YoY) and back-to-back record scan weeks, most recent at 12.1%.
Central tension: reconciling 37% reported Q1 revenue growth with ~70% IRI consumer sell-through - depressed by lapping a $20-25M artificial Pepsi inventory build in Q1 2023.
Management repeatedly stressed it cannot control Pepsi inventory decisions; reported revenue will 'catch up' to consumer demand 'whatever quarter that may be.'

Largest shelf resets in company history underway (~50% complete); convenience resets (the biggest opportunity given ~10% convenience share vs 68% of category sold there) delayed by labor shortages, expected done by June.
Margin guidance held in 'upper 40s' despite a 51%+ Q1 - constrained by reset-related slotting fees, trial promotions, and Essentials volume ramp.
Celsius Essentials (16-oz) proven incremental, rolling into convenience for the larger-can value segment; deliberately different branding to avoid cannibalizing core lines.

Pricing: Red Bull took a 2023 increase, Monster announced a Q4 2024 increase; Celsius declined to announce its own but said the team is 'very disciplined to take advantage' of pricing opportunity post-resets.
International: Canada at ~5.5% share / ~$25M run rate within months; North America remains the priority. Management declined to commit to Monster's ~40% five-year international mix.
'100 days of summer' positioned as the biggest in company history (MLS, F1/Ferrari, Jake Paul vs Mike Tyson fight, concert series).

Margin levers: 'orbit' one-day-delivery freight model and co-packer renegotiations as volume scales; long-term aspiration to reach Monster-like gross margins at scale, though margin focus deferred to drive scale first.
Red Bull terminated its longtime NYC distributor (going direct), framed by management as a potential opportunity for Celsius.
Asked, given decelerating energy-category scanner growth, what management views as the driver.

2023 was a high-comp year, so deceleration partly reflects lapping difficult comps - view on a two-year stack. Management remains bullish - Mintel anticipates ~8.8% category growth for the foreseeable future. The category is 'blurring' toward total beverage as usage occasions expand into daily lifestyle/routine; Celsius is bringing in new consumers.
Asked whether management is seeing any noticeable changes in consumption patterns amid the step-down in growth.

Data shows nothing significant; growth remains good. The brand is well positioned, bringing in new consumers and retaining consumers who would have aged out by positioning Celsius as a better fuel alternative. Still under-indexed in convenience (~68% of category sales); summer reset data will provide more clarity.
Noted Q1 2024 revenue growth of 37% (lapping 95%) and asked how growth is continuing into April and May.

The 37% is sell-in to Pepsi and other partners, depressed by a significant reduction in Pepsi days-on-hand and lapping a ~$20-25M artificial inventory build in Q1 2023; consumer sell-through (IRI) growth was ~70%. Management bullish - the brand continues to resonate and bring in new consumers; resets still underway.
Asked, given spring shelf-space gains, whether Pepsi will order more to fill the additional space.

~50% of resets complete; the biggest are still to come in convenience. Scan data should be the focus - registers strong, a record scan week at earnings release and a most-recent week at 12.1% share, two back-to-back record weeks. Convenience resets run through end of May, done by June. Celsius won a supplier award at Casey's.
Asked Pepsi's share of distribution and inventory levels with the rest of Celsius's distributors.

Pepsi is ~62% of North America distribution; the rest is direct to Amazon and club plus regional distributors. Non-Pepsi inventory is consistent. Underlying demand is strong; Celsius cannot control Pepsi inventory swings, but consumer demand will flow through and reported revenue will catch up. Pepsi days-of-supply will stay consistent (rising in dollars with revenue). Celsius optimized inventory by $47M over 15 months. NYC share is close to 20.
Noted possible changes with one of the big energy brands in the NYC market and a potential opportunity for Celsius.
Confirmed Red Bull terminated its longtime NYC distribution partner to go direct. Such disruption can create opportunity, and Celsius will try to make it an opportunistic situation.
Noted retailer feedback that Celsius is one of the biggest space gainers and asked about the ~50% reset visibility.

The huge opportunity is convenience, where Celsius has ~10% share versus higher elsewhere; 68% of energy drinks sell in convenience. Grocery and mass reset earlier; convenience resets somewhat delayed by labor shortages but the biggest opportunity. Focus: set resets, build the retail 'billboard,' secure secondary cold placements.
Asked for a sense of the percentage increase in retail space this year, comparison to prior year, whether it met internal expectations, and whether it can be quantified.

Declined an exact quantification but illustrated with examples - Publix and Kroger migrating Celsius from HBC to the beverage aisle. Celsius quadrupled its sales/key-accounts teams. On items per store, Celsius is ~20 versus 28%-30% for Monster/Red Bull; the bigger impact is improved placement ('out of the gutter,' 'bull's eye zone,' billboard, secondary placements). Household penetration ~29%, up over 11 points.
Convenience Reset Examples & Category Growth Share
Sought further color on the reset gains and how they compare to expectations.

No percentage given but ~50% of resets complete; this is the year of biggest gains ever. Circle K (second-largest convenience chain, ~13 divisions) had only ~half its divisions entered last year; in Florida Circle K, Celsius has 20-plus share in multiple markets but sits in the bottom-row gutter awaiting reset. Dollar General moved from warm to cold placements (~doubling availability); Maverik doubled space. Celsius drives ~47% of category growth.
Noting Red Bull's 2023 increase and Monster's announced Q4 2024 increase, asked whether Celsius would consider following on pricing.

Celsius constantly analyzes the market and does not want to be a drag; sees pricing opportunities going forward but timing and sequencing are critical, especially mid-resets. Launched Essentials 16-oz for convenience with promotional strategies for trial. Pricing/promotional architecture matters by channel and pack mix. Would not announce a price increase but said the team is disciplined to take advantage of pricing opportunity.
Asked, given Essentials is incremental, how much it has potentially cannibalized core brands.

Management ecstatic about Essentials' performance and incrementality since the Q4 2023 7-Eleven launch; it attracts a different consumer wanting more volume (16-oz can), with deliberately different branding/packaging to avoid cannibalization. Fieldly added the flavor profile is 'spot on.'
Asked for thoughts on stepped-up competition (Reign Storm, Bang, etc.) and how concerned management is.

The beverage industry is extremely competitive - ~1,000 new brands launch yearly and few reach $100M in sales. Celsius has a loyal consumer segment and amazing innovation/assets; it must stay true to its core, win consumers daily, and connect through culture - 'bigger than the liquid in the can,' analogizing to Nike.
Asked where Canada's ~5.5% share is coming from and how big the Canadian energy market is versus the US.

Management was surprised - the brand resonated very well. The US is the highest priority by size; Canada gets marketing spillover as a neighbor. The Canadian category is ~$500M at 100% capture, so a ~4%-5% share equals a ~$25M run rate; Canada is roughly the size of Ohio - reinforcing a methodical international approach.
Asked about other international expansion plans (Australia, France, Ireland, New Zealand, UK).

Celsius has signed distribution agreements and has product on the ground in the UK and Ireland, using a methodical timing-and-sequencing approach - launching in select retailers and the fitness channel to build a loyal base before scaling. Australia, France, New Zealand planned for Q4 2024. North America remains the priority; health-and-wellness trends are global.
Asked about the international route-to-market and the decision process for choosing partners.

Pepsi's international system is mostly third-party bottlers (with some Pepsi-owned, e.g., Canada, Germany); Celsius is not beholden to use them - giving negotiating leverage. Celsius signed multiple deals with Suntory, a Tier-one Australian distributor and #1 energy player there. Speculated Monster's large US/international gap may stem from fast-signed Coke-network deals ~10 years ago now nearing renegotiation. Celsius will pick the best partner per market.
International Revenue Mix Over Five Years
Asked how big international could become as a percentage of sales and how quickly Celsius can scale it.

Fieldly sees no reason Celsius could not reach a Monster-like revenue mix at maturity in 5-10 years. Toby David noted Monster was ~20% international at Celsius's current stage; Celsius will take it easy, judged quarterly by the street, and will not burn the P&L investing in too many markets at once - but with international properties like F1/Ferrari, growth could snowball. He declined to commit to Monster's ~40% international mix in five years.
Asked why management kept full-year gross margin guidance in the 'high 40% range' when Q1 came in over 51%, and where the upside lies.

Management does not want to commit above the upper-40s, especially with resets bringing margin constraints - slotting fees, trial promotions, and Essentials volume ramp; a reset shelf does not automatically fill the cart. Confident in the upper 40s. Margin levers include the orbit one-day-delivery freight model and co-packer renegotiations as volume scales.
Asked whether management has a longer-term gross margin aspiration beyond the high-40s 2024 guidance.

Management has long said it believes that upon scale gross margin can be similar to Monster, its largest peer; but said now is not the time to truly focus on margin impact - the priority is driving further scale within the category.
